readerTitle: Great products that make terrible businesses
caseNote: 가상 사례 (사내 데이터팀, 습관 앱, 거리 음악가) + 개념 출처 연구 (Brandenburger & Stuart, 1996)
insight: '얼마나 좋은가'와 '그중 얼마가 나에게 돌아오는가'는 서로 다른 질문이고, 사업은 두 번째 질문에도 답해야 살아남는다.
misconception: 정말 좋은 것을 만들면 돈과 인정은 저절로 따라온다.

sources.text: Brandenburger, A. M., & Stuart, H. W. (1996). Value-based Business Strategy. Journal of Economics & Management Strategy, 5(1), 5–24.
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 분해 카드 계산: 고객에게 주는 가치 $100 − 제공 비용 $20 = 만든 가치 $80. 가격 $30 − 비용 $20 = 내가 가져가는 몫 $10. $100 − $30 = 고객이 가져가는 몫 $70. $70 + $10 = $80으로 합이 맞습니다.
Brandenburger & Stuart(1996)가 가치를 '고객의 지불 의사 − 공급자의 기회비용'으로 정의하고, 이를 여러 참여자가 나눈다고 본 점을 원문으로 다시 확인하세요. 카드에는 '1990s'와 일반적인 설명만 적었습니다.

cards.title: Everyone loved the dashboard. Then it got cut.
body: A three-person data team inside a retail company built a dashboard. Within a year, 300 colleagues opened it every morning. Store managers used it to order stock. Finance used it to close the month faster.
At the budget review, the team was cut in half. Nobody disputed that the tool was good. It was simply hard to say what the company got back for paying for it.

image.label: Office workers around a glowing dashboard while an empty budget folder sits aside
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 사무실에서 여러 사람이 큰 모니터 속 대시보드를 즐겁게 보고 있고, 한쪽 구석 책상에는 'Budget' 라벨이 붙은 거의 빈 폴더가 놓여 있음. 실제 회사 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You lead the data team. The next budget review is in three months.
body: The dashboard is popular, but your budget looks like pure cost to finance. You have time for one main push before the review.

options.text: Build the three features users ask for most, so the tool is even better
options.feedback: Users get happier, but the budget problem stays the same. You'd be adding more value that still flows to other teams without anything coming back.

options.text: Track the decisions the dashboard changed and what they saved, and ask the teams that rely on it to fund part of it
options.feedback: This links the value you create to something that returns to your team: credit, proof and money. It costs build time now, but it answers the question finance is really asking.

options.text: Run a survey showing how much colleagues love the tool
options.feedback: Love is a good sign that value exists. But a survey shows people like it, not what the company gets back for funding it.

cards.title: The value was real. It just landed somewhere else.
body: Store managers ordered less waste. Finance saved days each month. Those gains showed up in *other* teams' results.
The data team's own line in the budget showed only salaries and software. The good they did was spread across the company, and none of it was counted back to them.
The tool didn't fail. The arrangement around it did.

cards.title: Creating value vs capturing value
body: **Creating value** means making someone better off by more than it costs you to do it. **Capturing value** means keeping a share of that gain for yourself, as a price, a profit, a budget or credit.
They are two separate questions. Strategy researchers Adam Brandenburger and Harborne Stuart framed it this way in the 1990s: first value is created, then it gets divided among the people involved.

image.label: A pie of value split between the customer and the business
image.brief: 큰 파이 하나에 'Value created' 라벨. 파이가 두 조각으로 나뉘어 큰 조각은 'Customer keeps', 작은 조각은 'Business captures'. 파이 크기와 조각 나누기가 다른 문제라는 점이 보이게.

cards.title: One product, three numbers.
body: A service is worth $100 to a customer. It costs you $20 to provide, and you charge $30. Together you created **$80** of value. The customer keeps $70. You keep $10.

cards.title: The gap shows up on every street.
body: A street musician fills a square with music for 200 people. Five drop coins. A lot of value was created. Very little was captured.

The same gap hits a bakery whose recipe gets copied, or a consultant whose free advice wins the client's deal. Being good decides how big the pie is. Something else decides how much you get: a price people must pay, something hard to copy, or a clear link between your work and the gain.

image.label: A crowd enjoying a street musician with an almost empty hat
image.brief: 광장에서 거리 음악가 주변에 많은 사람이 즐겁게 모여 있고, 바닥의 모자에는 동전 몇 개뿐. 따뜻한 색감, 사람들 표정은 행복하게.

cards.title: Capture too much, and you stop creating.
body: The fix is not to grab the whole pie. If you take nearly all the value, customers have little reason to choose you over the next option, and they leave when one appears.

Capture also comes second. Squeezing harder on a small pie rarely beats growing the pie and keeping a fair slice. The goal is a share big enough to keep you going and small enough that customers still feel ahead.

cards.title: Now it's a free app.
body: Your free habit-tracking app has 50,000 daily users and great reviews. Servers and two developers cost more each month than you earn, which is nothing.

options.text: Keep it fully free and focus on growth. Money will follow once you're big
options.feedback: Growth makes the pie bigger, but nothing in the plan turns any of it into revenue. Costs often grow with users, so the gap can widen.

options.text: Keep the core free and charge for the features your most active users rely on
options.feedback: You capture value where it's largest while most users still come out ahead. Some free users may grumble, but you finally have a way to survive.
Ads do capture some value, often from advertisers rather than users. But too many can shrink the value users get, and with it the habit you built.

cards.title: Making something great and getting paid for it are two different jobs.
body: First ask how much better off you make people. Then ask, separately, how much of that comes back to you, and why.
**Try it today:** pick one thing your business or team does well. Write down who gains from it, roughly how much, and what share returns to you.
